title: Parallel classical simulation of noisy shallow circuits: no quantum advantage in 1D
abstract: We consider quantum circuits consisting of $d$ layers of nearest-neighbor two-qubit gates acting on $n$ qubits arranged on a line, where every qubit is independently depolarized with a constant probability before each layer. We describe a randomized parallel algorithm which samples from the output distribution of any such circuit to within total variation error $δ$, with parallel runtime $2^{O(d)}\log\log(n/δ)$ and $n 2^{O(d)}$ elementary real-arithmetic operations. Without noise, the same approach gives an exact sampler with parallel runtime $O(\log n)$. For constant depth, we further show that the input/output behavior of the noisy quantum circuit is reproduced up to a constant error by a randomized $\mathsf{AC}^0$-circuit, that is, a Boolean circuit of polynomial size and constant depth with unbounded fan-in AND and OR gates and NOT gates. Consequently, every relation problem solved by a noisy constant-depth quantum circuit in one dimension is also solved, with essentially the same success probability, by a randomized $\mathsf{AC}^0$-circuit. This rules out, for noisy circuits in one dimension, the unconditional quantum advantage established for noisy shallow circuits in two and three dimensions, where polynomial-size classical circuits over the same gate set require depth $Ω(\log n/\log\log n)$. Our algorithm exploits the fact that depolarizing noise cuts a one-dimensional circuit into independent pieces of logarithmic width, each of which can be sampled exactly in parallel.
summary: This paper provides a classical simulation algorithm for noisy shallow quantum circuits on a 1D lattice. By exploiting the structure imposed by depolarizing noise, the authors show that the problem can be mapped onto a randomized AC^0 circuit. This result demonstrates that for 1D systems, the quantum advantage previously claimed for noisy shallow circuits in higher dimensions does not hold.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether a quantum advantage exists for simulating noisy, shallow quantum circuits in one dimension (1D) compared to classical computation.
main_result: It shows that for 1D noisy circuits, the output distribution can be simulated by a randomized AC^0 circuit, ruling out the unconditional quantum advantage established for 2D/3D noisy shallow circuits.
method: The authors develop randomized parallel algorithms and construct equivalent randomized Boolean circuits (AC^0) to sample the output distribution of the noisy quantum circuit.
model_or_system: The model consists of quantum circuits with $d$ layers of nearest-neighbor two-qubit gates acting on $n$ qubits arranged linearly, subjected to independent depolarizing noise before each layer.
key_observables: Total variation error ($\delta$), parallel runtime, and classical circuit depth/size.
important_parameters: Circuit depth ($d$), system size ($n$), noise probability ($p$), and error tolerance ($\delta$).
main_assumptions: The result is specific to 1D geometry and depolarizing noise; the simulation relies on the local effect of noise cutting the circuit into independent pieces.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates a three-layer brickwork circuit on 18 qubits showing the depolarizing noise channel at each location.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by analyzing the simulation complexity, first deriving bounds for general randomized Boolean circuits ($C_2$), then improving the structure to unbounded fan-in circuits ($C_\infty$), and finally achieving constant-depth simulation using lookup tables ($C_{lit}$).
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, constructive classical simulation technique for a class of quantum circuits, directly challenging the premise of quantum advantage in a specific, physically relevant setting (1D).
